newsitem.title: FRANCE: PSA sees difficult market conditions.
newsitem.headline: PSA sees difficult market conditions.

text.p: PSA Peugeot Citroen chairman Jacques Calvet said on Tuesday that the outlook for the European car market was grim but he said his group would not announce price-cutting measures in response to those set last week by rival Renault SA.

"As for 1997, forecasts are still very pessimistic with no expected growth," Calvet told a news conference. "The causes are primarily related to the convergence of European economic policies designed, no matter what they say, to meet the Maastricht criteria (for a single European currency)," he told a news conference at the Paris car show.

"While these policies might in the end encourage economic recovery in Europe, in the very short term they are sure to cause stagnation, since Europe is currently in a period of deflation, even if this term is sometimes contested," he said.

"These market conditions -- little growth in 1996 and none in 1997 -- have incited all carmakers to take actions to gain volume share at the expense of margins -- actions that are individually understandable but collectively dangerous," he said.
However, he said, despite the difficult outlook, the group was confident about its future thanks to product launches that allowed it this year to maintain its market share in Europe.
The PSA group is displaying new Peugeot 406 coupe and stationwagons at the car show, 406 sedan and Citroen Xantia models equipped with V6 engines, and three Citroen concept cars.
Calvet said the company had no plans to match Renault's decision announced last week to lower car prices through outright reductions or by adding equipment at no extra charge.
"We have always considered that our role was to discern the tastes of our clients...in terms of price, security, quality, technology," he said. "It's what we've been doing for years."
Company officials said the Peugeot and Citroen divisions prepared model ranges adapted to a market expected to weaken sharply after the expiry yesterday of a French state rebate scheme.
Calvet said the latest forecasts for 1996 were for a five percent increase in the European car market, helped by a state rebate programme in France.
But even with that gain, the industry will have recovered only around 60 percent of the market plunge in 1993, he said.

Calvet said he regretted that the government had not agreed to further measures to assist the French car industry, given the heavy fiscal burdens imposed on the industry through value-added tax of 20.6 percent, petrol and other taxes.

But company officials said the group was on track to meet its objective to increase sales outside western Europe to 25 percent of the total by the year 2000. Citroen expects its car sales outside Europe to reach 80,000 this year and 100,000 in 1997, and Peugeot expects its sales outside Europe to total around 186,000 this year and over 200,000 next year.
Calvet said the group was studying expanding production in Latin America and possibly setting up production in Brazil.
He said the group had not arrived at a decision on whether to attempt production in North America. "We're focusing more on South America," he said.
